note.text:
Numbers do three different jobs.
• A cardinal number tells us how many: 'There are 12 mangoes in the basket.'
• An ordinal number tells us the position or order: 'Enow came 3rd in the race.' We write ordinals as 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th … or first, second, third, fourth …
• A nominal number is a name or label. It does not count anything: a phone number, the number on a taxi, a football shirt number.

Ask yourself: does it count? Cardinal. Does it give a position? Ordinal. Is it only a label? Nominal.

Endings of ordinals: numbers ending in 1 take st (21st), ending in 2 take nd (32nd), ending in 3 take rd (43rd), and the others take th (57th). But numbers ending in 11, 12 or 13 always take th: 11th, 12th, 113th.

worked_example.problem: There are {n} people in a queue at the Mile Two taxi park. Mbah is {ordinal(p)} from the front. What is his position from the back?
steps: People in front of Mbah: {p} − {one} = {p - one}.
From the back, Mbah comes just after those {n - p} people, so his position is {n - p} + {one} = {n - p + one}.
worked_example.answer: Mbah is {ordinal(n - p + one)} from the back.

cards.idea: A cardinal number tells how many.
example: {n} tells how many mangoes: it is a cardinal number.

check.prompt: Which sentence uses a cardinal number (a number that tells how many)?

right.text: There are {n} pupils in the class.

wrong.explain: {ordinal(k)} gives a position: it is an ordinal number.

wrong.text: The number painted on the taxi is {plate}.
wrong.explain: A taxi number is only a label: it is a nominal number.
A shirt number is only a label: it is a nominal number.

cards.idea: An ordinal number tells a position: first, second, third… In figures: {ordinal(1)}, {ordinal(2)}, {ordinal(3)}, {ordinal(4)}.
example: But {ordinal(11)}, {ordinal(12)} and {ordinal(13)} always end in th.

cards.idea: A nominal number is only a name or label. It does not count anything and does not give an order.
example: {plate} does not count anything, and the taxi is not the {ordinal(plate)} of anything: it is a nominal number.

pick.text: There are {n} pupils in Form One B.
Ngwa bought {n} oranges at the market.
Ewane finished {ordinal(k)} in the inter-class race.
Today is the {ordinal(k)} day of the month.
The number painted on the taxi is {plate}.
Bih wears shirt number {k} in the school football team.

questions.prompt: In the sentence “{s.text}”, the number is:

misconceptions.explain: A cardinal number answers 'how many?'. Here the number is {s.kind}.
An ordinal number gives a position: 1st, 2nd, 3rd… Here the number is {s.kind}.
A nominal number is only a label, like a phone or taxi number. Here the number is {s.kind}.

solution: Does the number count something? Cardinal. Does it give a position? Ordinal. Is it only a label? Nominal.

questions.prompt: How do you write '{words(n)}' as an ordinal number in figures?

misconceptions.explain: Numbers ending in 1, 2 or 3 take st, nd or rd (21st, 32nd, 43rd), except those ending in 11, 12 or 13, which take th.
Look at the last digit: 1 → st, 2 → nd, 3 → rd, others → th. But 11, 12 and 13 always take th.

solution: Numbers ending in {11}, {12} or {13} take th. Otherwise a last digit of {1} takes st, {2} takes nd, {3} takes rd.

questions.prompt: {n} people are in a queue at the Mile Two taxi park. Mbah is {ordinal(p)} from the front. In which position is he from the back? (Give the number only.)

misconceptions.explain: {n - p} people are behind Mbah. He comes just after them: {n - p} + 1.
His position from the back is different: count the people behind him, then add 1 for Mbah.

solution: From the back he comes just after them: {n - p} + {1} = {n - p + 1}.

questions.prompt: In a race, Tabe finished {ordinal(p)}. {m} runners finished after him. How many runners were in the race?

misconceptions.explain: Being {ordinal(p)} means {p - 1} runners finished before Tabe. Add them, Tabe and the {m} after him: {p - 1} + 1 + {m}.
Tabe is already counted in '{ordinal(p)}': the total is {p} + {m}.

solution: Finishing {ordinal(p)} means {p - 1} runners finished before Tabe.
